prompt.context: Our client is a major TV Network. They want to know how much to bid on the TV rights for the 2016 Olympic Games. The bid will need to be paid in 2010. The total programming is 16 days: Opening Ceremonies on a Friday 8pm–11pm, 14 days of programming for 10 hours a day (9am–12pm, 2pm–5pm, and 7pm–11pm on weekdays; 11am–9pm on weekends), and Closing Ceremony on the following Saturday 8pm–11pm. This only includes rights to U.S. programming; overseas programming is out of scope. The network will only show the Olympics on their one flagship channel. Olympic programming will replace regularly scheduled programming. Prime time is considered anytime after 7pm on a weekday and all day during the weekends.
prompt.question: How much should our client bid for the 2016 Olympic TV rights (bid paid in 2010)?

clarifying_info.q: What is the ad rate for prime time?
What is the ad rate for non-prime time?
How much ad time is there per hour?
clarifying_info.a: 10 minutes of ads per hour (both prime and non-prime)

clarifying_info.q: What are the costs to cover the Olympics?
clarifying_info.a: $428M total cost (includes all fixed and variable costs for travel, equipment, salaries, etc.)

clarifying_info.q: What is the opportunity cost of replacing regular programming?
What discount rate should we use for time value of money?

exhibits.title: Breakdown of Ad Revenue and Costs during Olympics
exhibits.shows: A structured breakdown showing prime time vs. non-prime time ad rates and ad minutes per hour, alongside a breakdown of costs including coverage costs and opportunity cost of displaced programming

framework: Calculate total prime time programming hours during the 16-day window
Calculate total non-prime time programming hours during the 16-day window
Compute ad revenue from each tier (hours × ad minutes × rate per 30s × 2)
Calculate total costs: coverage cost ($428M) + opportunity cost ($1M × total hours)
Derive 2016 profit = total revenue − total costs
Discount 2016 profit back to 2010 using cost of capital (Rule of 72 shortcut at 12%)
Adjust final bid upward or downward for strategic factors (future viewership bump, required margin)

questions.prompt: How many prime time and non-prime time programming hours are there across the 16 days?
questions.guidance: Strong candidates quickly identify the schedule structure rather than listing every day. There are 10 weekdays and 4 weekend days in the 14-day block, plus the Friday opening (3 prime-time hrs) and Saturday closing (3 prime-time hrs). Weekday prime time = 7pm–11pm = 4 hrs/day × 10 days = 40 hrs. Weekday non-prime = 9am–12pm + 2pm–5pm = 6 hrs/day × 10 days = 60 hrs. Weekend all-day = 11am–9pm = 10 hrs/day × 4 days = 40 hrs (all prime). Opening + Closing = 3 + 3 = 6 hrs (all prime). Total prime = 40 + 40 + 6 = 86 hrs. Total non-prime = 60 hrs.

math.setup: Weekday prime (7pm-11pm): 4 hrs × 10 days = 40 hrs. Weekend (11am-9pm, all prime): 10 hrs × 4 days = 40 hrs. Opening + Closing ceremonies (3 hrs each, both prime): 6 hrs. Total prime = 86 hrs. Weekday non-prime (9am-12pm + 2pm-5pm = 6 hrs): 6 hrs × 10 days = 60 hrs. Total non-prime = 60 hrs.
steps: Prime time hours = 40 (weekday evenings) + 40 (weekend days) + 6 (ceremonies) = 86 hrs
Non-prime time hours = 6 hrs/day × 10 weekdays = 60 hrs
math.answer: 86 prime time hours, 60 non-prime time hours, 146 total hours

questions.prompt: What is the total ad revenue the network will earn during the 2016 Olympics?
questions.guidance: 10 min of ads per hour = 20 slots of 30 seconds. Revenue = slots × rate. Multiply by hours for each tier. Prime: 86 hrs × 20 slots × $400k = $688M. Non-prime: 60 hrs × 20 slots × $200k = $240M. Total = $928M.

math.setup: Ad slots per hour = 10 min × 2 slots per min = 20 slots of 30 sec. Prime revenue = prime hrs × 20 × $400k. Non-prime revenue = non-prime hrs × 20 × $200k.

questions.prompt: What are the total costs (coverage + opportunity cost)?
questions.guidance: Coverage cost is given as $428M. Opportunity cost = $1M per programming hour × 146 total hours = $146M. Total costs = $428M + $146M = $574M.

questions.prompt: What is the 2016 profit, and what is the maximum bid the network should make today (2010)?
questions.guidance: 2016 profit = $928M − $574M = $354M. The bid is paid in 2010, so we must discount $354M back 6 years. At 12% cost of capital, use Rule of 72: 72 / 12 = 6 years to double → $354M in 2016 is worth ~$177M in 2010 (half the 2016 value). Strong candidates recognize the Rule of 72 shortcut and apply it cleanly.

math.setup: 2016 profit = Revenue − Costs. Discount to 2010 using Rule of 72 at 12% CoC: money doubles every 72/12 = 6 years, so 2016 value ÷ 2 = 2010 value.
steps: $354M received in 6 years is worth $354M / 2 = $177M today (2010)

brainstorming.prompt: What additional factors should the network consider when adjusting the bid above or below $177M?

categories.name: Revenue upside
ideas: Increased viewership on the flagship channel spills over to other programs, boosting future ad rates
Sponsorship and partnership deals tied to Olympic coverage
Halo effect: advertisers willing to pay premium for association with the Olympics

categories.name: Cost/risk factors
ideas: Potential cost overruns on production and travel
Currency or scheduling risk if games are delayed or disrupted
Competitive bids driving rights cost above NPV

categories.name: Strategic value
ideas: Brand prestige and network positioning vs. competitors
Audience demographics of Olympic viewers (attractive to advertisers)
Anchor programming effect: Olympic viewers may stay for surrounding content
First-mover advantage if rival networks win the rights

categories.name: Financial adjustments
ideas: Sensitivity analysis on ad rates (could be higher or lower in 2016)
Required return hurdle rate may differ from 12%
Time value uncertainty if cost of capital changes

recommendation: The network should bid up to approximately $177M for the 2016 Olympic TV rights, representing the net present value of an estimated $354M profit generated during the games discounted at 12% over 6 years
The bid may be adjusted upward if the network assigns significant value to halo viewership effects, brand positioning, or advertiser relationships that extend beyond the games themselves
risks: Actual ad revenue may fall short if Olympic viewership underperforms historical benchmarks
Production and travel costs could exceed the $428M estimate
A competing network may bid higher, making the opportunity cost of losing the rights strategically significant
next_steps: Conduct sensitivity analysis on prime-time viewership ratings and ad rates to bound the revenue estimate
Assess historical Olympic ratings trends to refine the $354M profit estimate
Evaluate strategic value of Olympic rights to the network's long-term brand and advertiser relationships before finalizing the bid
